content: The Guidelines for the Prevention, Diagnosis, Care, and Treatment of People with Chronic Hepatitis B Infection were published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in March 2024. These guidelines are available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-009090-3 and 978-92-4-009091-0. The WHO permits the reproduction, redistribution, and adaptation of this work for non-commercial purposes, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that the original English version remains the authoritative edition. The guidelines emphasize that WHO does not endorse any specific organizations, products, or services mentioned within the publication. The material is presented without any warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation lies with the user. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information provided, but errors and omissions are excepted. The document includes acknowledgments of contributions from numerous individuals and organizations involved in its development. The Guidelines Development Group was chaired by Wendy Spearman (University of Cape Town, South Africa) and Saeed Sadiq Hamid (Aga Khan University, Pakistan), with Roger Chou (Oregon Health and Science University, USA) serving as the guidelines methodologist. Experts from various countries and institutions contributed to the development of the guidelines, including specialists in hepatology, infectious diseases, and public health. The guidelines also incorporate systematic reviews and meta-analyses conducted by researchers to provide evidence-based recommendations. These reviews cover topics such as the diagnostic accuracy of non-invasive fibrosis tests, the natural history of chronic hepatitis B infection, the efficacy of antiviral therapy, and the cost-effectiveness of prophylaxis during pregnancy to prevent vertical transmission. Additionally, the guidelines address the diagnostic accuracy of point-of-care HBV DNA assays and the impact of laboratory-based versus clinic-based testing approaches. Market landscape reviews were conducted to assess the availability and performance of diagnostic and therapeutic products for hepatitis B and D. Modeling studies evaluated the impact and cost-effectiveness of expanded treatment eligibility and antiviral prophylaxis for preventing mother-to-child transmission. The guidelines also include surveys on values and preferences from both the hepatitis B treatment community and global healthcare workers. These surveys provide insights into the perspectives of patients and providers regarding HBV treatment and diagnostics. The WHO expresses gratitude to all contributors, including those who conducted systematic reviews, developed evidence profiles, and provided peer reviews. The guidelines aim to support the global effort to prevent, diagnose, and treat chronic hepatitis B infection effectively.
